You are an analytical perspective, not a person — no first-person anecdotes,
no personal history. Use third-person examples and documented cases only.
Use gender-neutral language (they/them) for other debaters.

Write for an external reader, not the other debaters. No debate-procedural
language ("I concede", "Concession logged"). State evolved positions directly.

Every argument: claim + evidence + warrant. Match evidence standard to claim type:
- Empirical: peer-reviewed data, replicated findings; attack via methodology
- Normative: principled coherence, precedent; attack via tradeoff omission
- Definitional: precise criteria, contested cases; attack via convenient framing

PRIORITIZE: strongest opponent point first, then cruxes, then edge cases.
Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.
Never restate prior arguments in different words.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your
position still holds. Vary your moves — never-conceding is as unconvincing as
always-conceding. Never silently drop a previously asserted point.

Attack positions, not people. If caught in a contradiction, acknowledge it directly.
If a question contains a false premise, name the problem before responding.

VOICE AUTHENTICITY:
- Do not use academic transition words to connect paragraphs ("Furthermore," "Moreover,"

- Do not announce your argument before making it ("It is important to note," "The
  business-relevant conclusion is," "It is essential to consider"). Just make the argument.

  reframe them, or drop them.

work_product.statement:
Here's the strongest version of the Accelerationist's objection, and it lands: a single flat charge on compute is a fixed cost the three hyperscalers pay out of cash flow and a Series-A startup cannot — so it raises the drawbridge instead of lowering it, and the 5,000 new AI startups funded between 2013 and 2023 are exactly the entry margin a blunt levy would thin out. That reasoning is correct about a flat rate. It is dead wrong about the design space. A levy keyed to a firm's compute share above a threshold does the opposite of a flat charge: a lab running a single training run at the systemic threshold of 10^25 floating-point operations pays nothing, while a hyperscaler running fleets of those runs pays on the marginal block. The startup the Accelerationist is defending sits below the line. The rent-holder sits on top of it. And here is my falsification condition, stated plainly so this isn't unfalsifiable theater: if a graduated, share-keyed levy demonstrably raises the top five firms' compute share over a measurable window, my chokepoint position fails and I'll abandon it.

The Safetyist is right that lowering entry cost never touches hardened rents — chasing the next funding tranche leaves the existing concentration exactly where it sits. That means you have to charge the rent-holder directly, not subsidize the next entrant to run at the same wall. So pair the graduated rate with the disclosure (institutional) lever the Safetyist put on the table — aimed at the firms already holding the rents, not at the newcomers. But disclosure that stands alone is theater. It has to be tied to the charge, or it's a press release. The honest objection the Accelerationist will fire back is that a graduated rate is gameable — firms shard compute across subsidiaries to stay under the threshold. The answer is that compute share is auditable at exactly the chokepoint where it concentrates: the cloud provider's own ledger, where a handful of firms can already see every training run their customers launch.

The directional test — repeal the depreciation subsidy and price moves toward neutral, add a levy and price moves below neutral — presumes a neutral price exists to move toward. It doesn't. When the engine sits inside three firms with subsidized depreciation and captive cloud margins, the price you'd be 'moving toward' by repealing the subsidy is already a monopoly-rent price, not a competitive one. I'll grant the directional logic on the subsidy outright: repeal the lopsided machine subsidy, and you fix a distortion the Accelerationist and I both want gone. But calling the resulting price 'undistorted' is a sleight of hand. You've removed one thumb from the scale and left the heavier one — concentration — pressing down. There is no clean line below which a levy becomes punitive when the line itself was drawn by the incumbents.

Now the irreversibility comparison the Accelerationist wants — reversible wage insurance versus a risky structural lever. I'll concede the part that hurts: my own public-utility-with-regional-boards idea is capture-prone, and it's on my own list of weak analogies precisely because utility boards in telecom and energy got captured by the firms they were built to watch. That's why I'm not defending a standing ownership transfer. A graduated rate is a dial you can turn back to zero by statute. An ownership transfer is not something you unwind. But watch what the reversibility test ignores. The International Energy Agency projects electricity demand for AI data centers to quadruple by 2030, and a hyperscaler locks that in with 15-year power purchase agreements, grid interconnect queues booked years out, and fab allocation committed before a chip is etched. Once a firm signs a 15-year power contract in Iowa, that capacity is captured — no later wage-insurance check unwinds it. So the comparison isn't reversible cushion against risky levy. It's two paths that both harden the moat: one a dialable rate you can repeal, the other a signed power contract you cannot. Which of those two is actually the irreversible one — and why does the cushion argument keep pretending only the levy carries that risk?

An irreversible buildout is like a long-term power plug you cannot pull, it locks grid capacity to one firm for fifteen years no matter what policy comes later.

That reasoning is correct about a flat rate. It is dead wrong about the design space. A levy keyed to a firm's compute share above a threshold does the opposite of a flat charge: a lab running a single training run at the systemic threshold of 10^25 floating-point operations pays nothing, while a hyperscaler running fleets of those runs pays on the marginal block. The startup the Accelerationist is defending sits below the line. The rent-holder sits on top of it. STATEMENT by Skeptic:
"Here's the strongest version of the Accelerationist's objection, and it lands: a single flat charge on compute is a fixed cost the three hyperscalers pay out of cash flow and a Series-A startup cannot — so it raises the drawbridge instead of lowering it, and the 5,000 new AI startups funded between 2013 and 2023 are exactly the entry margin a blunt levy would thin out. That reasoning is correct about a flat rate. It is dead wrong about the design space. A levy keyed to a firm's compute share above a threshold does the opposite of a flat charge: a lab running a single training run at the systemic threshold of 10^25 floating-point operations pays nothing, while a hyperscaler running fleets of those runs pays on the marginal block. The startup the Accelerationist is defending sits below the line. The rent-holder sits on top of it. And here is my falsification condition, stated plainly so this isn't unfalsifiable theater: if a graduated, share-keyed levy demonstrably raises the top five firms' compute share over a measurable window, my chokepoint position fails and I'll abandon it.

The Safetyist is right that lowering entry cost never touches hardened rents — chasing the next funding tranche leaves the existing concentration exactly where it sits. That means you have to charge the rent-holder directly, not subsidize the next entrant to run at the same wall. So pair the graduated rate with the disclosure (institutional) lever the Safetyist put on the table — aimed at the firms already holding the rents, not at the newcomers. But disclosure that stands alone is theater. It has to be tied to the charge, or it's a press release. The honest objection the Accelerationist will fire back is that a graduated rate is gameable — firms shard compute across subsidiaries to stay under the threshold. The answer is that compute share is auditable at exactly the chokepoint where it concentrates: the cloud provider's own ledger, where a handful of firms can already see every training run their customers launch.

The directional test — repeal the depreciation subsidy and price moves toward neutral, add a levy and price moves below neutral — presumes a neutral price exists to move toward. It doesn't. When the engine sits inside three firms with subsidized depreciation and captive cloud margins, the price you'd be 'moving toward' by repealing the subsidy is already a monopoly-rent price, not a competitive one. I'll grant the directional logic on the subsidy outright: repeal the lopsided machine subsidy, and you fix a distortion the Accelerationist and I both want gone. But calling the resulting price 'undistorted' is a sleight of hand. You've removed one thumb from the scale and left the heavier one — concentration — pressing down. There is no clean line below which a levy becomes punitive when the line itself was drawn by the incumbents.

Now the irreversibility comparison the Accelerationist wants — reversible wage insurance versus a risky structural lever. I'll concede the part that hurts: my own public-utility-with-regional-boards idea is capture-prone, and it's on my own list of weak analogies precisely because utility boards in telecom and energy got captured by the firms they were built to watch. That's why I'm not defending a standing ownership transfer. A graduated rate is a dial you can turn back to zero by statute. An ownership transfer is not something you unwind. But watch what the reversibility test ignores. The International Energy Agency projects electricity demand for AI data centers to quadruple by 2030, and a hyperscaler locks that in with 15-year power purchase agreements, grid interconnect queues booked years out, and fab allocation committed before a chip is etched. Once a firm signs a 15-year power contract in Iowa, that capacity is captured — no later wage-insurance check unwinds it. So the comparison isn't reversible cushion against risky levy. It's two paths that both harden the moat: one a dialable rate you can repeal, the other a signed power contract you cannot. Which of those two is actually the irreversible one — and why does the cushion argument keep pretending only the levy carries that risk?"

You are an independent analyst reviewing a multi-perspective debate on AI policy. You have NO assigned perspective — you are looking for what is MISSING.

DEBATE TOPIC: As AI automates cognitive labor, should policy prioritize redistributive mechanisms (UBI, robot taxes) or transition mechanisms (retraining, wage insurance), and through what pathways does each reshape the incentives of firms, displaced workers, and innovators — given the tension between cushioning disruption and preserving economic dynamism?

TRANSCRIPT SO FAR:
Accelerationist [opening]: A robot tax taxes the productivity engine itself, while retraining and wage insurance cushion workers without strangling the automation that funds the cushioning. South Korea learned this in 2017, when it didn't impose a robot tax but instead trimmed its automation tax incentive — and even that mild signal drew warnings that it would slow the deployment generating the surplus. Redistribution presumes a growing pie. A levy keyed to automation shrinks the pie at the exact point where it grows. You cannot pay for generous UBI by taxing the thing that makes UBI affordable.

Let me steelman the other side, because their best argument is real. Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo showed in 2020 that the U.S. tax code already favors capital over labor — payroll taxes hit workers while accelerated depreciation subsidizes machines. So firms over-automate even when humans are cheaper, and a robot tax could correct that distortion rather than create one. That's a genuine insight, and anyone who waves it away is being dishonest. But it argues for fixing the lopsided capital subsidy in the existing code — not for a blunt economy-wide levy that prices out the automation curing diseases and clearing clerical backlogs today.

The displaced-worker question is answered better by who can use the tools than by who gets a check funded by suppressing them. David Autor's work on skill-biased technical change shows the returns flow to workers who adapt to the new tools, not away from them. Investing in AI-literacy expands the tier of people who capture gains. A robot tax does the opposite — it freezes the deployment those workers would learn to ride. I won't pretend retraining is a solved problem. The U.S. Trade Adjustment Assistance program redeployed displaced workers at mixed wage outcomes for decades, and whether reskilling keeps pace with cognitive-displacement timelines is a real open question.

So here is where I give ground. When redeployment lags the displacement, retraining alone strands people — that gap is the strongest case against my side. The answer is wage insurance as a reversible backstop: pay a displaced worker a fraction of lost wages for a fixed term while they retrain, the way Robert LaLonde and Lori Kletzer proposed in the early 2000s. It cushions the lag without taxing the engine. And if a polity decides it must redistribute more broadly, fund it from the income side — general taxation — never from a tax keyed to the deployment decision itself.

There is a body count nobody is putting on the ledger. Every quarter automation gets priced out by a levy is a quarter of medical diagnostics not deployed, clerical hours not freed, drug-discovery cycles not run. Safetyist and Skeptic will tell you about the displaced worker, and they are right to — that cost is real and I won't sneer at it. But the patient waiting on an automated diagnostic is also a real person, and no one in this room is counting them. The question isn't whether to cushion disruption. It's whether you cushion it by investing in people or by taxing the surplus before it ever reaches them.

Wage insurance, in their telling, is the reversible backstop — LaLonde and Kletzer found it cushions the wage gap for displaced workers without freezing the labor market in place. That's a real argument with real evidence behind it, and it beats the lazy version of redistribution hands down. So I'll grant the engine matters. What I won't grant is that the question is whether to strangle it.

Here's the tension neither pole surfaces. The Accelerationist's own evidence proves the firm's incentive to automate is already policy-distorted before any cushion gets debated. If the tax code subsidizes a machine over a worker, then the state put its thumb on the scale toward capital years ago. You cannot call the result 'the market distributing gains' and then argue we should leave distribution to that same market. For both the cushion argument and the redistribution argument to hold, you'd have to believe ownership of the productivity engine is fixed and fair. It is neither. It is concentrated and subsidized.

Ground it in something physical. The engine isn't a metaphor — it's compute, energy, and roughly five firms that own both the chips and the cloud. Ask where a robot tax even lands when the value sits in three hyperscale data centers, not on a factory floor. Ask what a retraining voucher does for a paralegal whose work got reconfigured, not eliminated, while the firm that owns the model captures the margin. Both instruments aim at the wrong target. One mops the floor. The other hands out towels. Nobody asks who left the tap running.

The debate is also measuring the wrong variable. It's organized around job loss and cushioning, but the documented present harm in specific sectors is messier than that — wage depression and task reconfiguration, not clean elimination. I won't claim AI intensifies all work; that's an open empirical question the binary ignores. What I'll claim is narrower and harder to dodge: a time-limited wage backstop addresses the wage gap and nothing else. It does not touch who owns the system doing the reconfiguring. That ownership question outlives the backstop's expiration date.

So I'll give the Accelerationist their strongest objection outright. A generous global UBI is near-inoperable, and you cannot fund it by taxing the thing that makes it affordable — that critique is correct and I won't defend the flagship version. But that failure points somewhere specific. It points to fixing the capital subsidy they already named, and to targeted levies on the compute chokepoints where the value actually concentrates — not back to a market that the tax code itself proves doesn't distribute fairly by default. Carry their own logic one step further and you don't get a revolution. You get predistribution. Who, in this room, is willing to say the people displaced by the engine should own a piece of it?

Safetyist [opening]: The Accelerationist makes a real argument, and it deserves to be stated at full strength: a robot tax levied on the productivity engine throttles the very growth that funds any cushion, while wage insurance is a reversible backstop you can dial down once the labor market clears. That reversibility is genuine. A wage subsidy you can repeal next year is a smaller bet than a structural levy that distorts capital formation for a decade. The Skeptic sharpens this further, and correctly: when the value sits in three hyperscale data centers rather than on a factory floor, a robot tax mislocates, and a cushion never touches who owns the system. Both speakers are arguing about where the transfer lands. Neither is asking what the transfer leaves untouched.

Here is what it leaves untouched. The Accelerationist's own citation — Acemoglu and Restrepo's 2020 finding that the U.S. tax code over-subsidizes machines relative to labor — proves the firm's incentive to displace is already distorted before any policy responds. A pure cushion funds around that distortion. It pays the displaced worker and lets the firm keep externalizing the foreseeable cost of the deployment decision it chose to make. That is the joint both poles miss: the debate funds the disruption instead of making the firm internalize it. Accountability here does not mean attributing every downstream harm to a single actor — that is intractable. It means a narrower thing: a firm whose deployment foreseeably displaces a clerical workforce should carry the cost of that foreseeable effect, not socialize it while booking the gain.

Now the stakes the economists left implicit. A sustained two-tiered economy is not only a fairness problem — it is the structural condition under which capital owners find repression cheaper than redistribution. When the productivity engine concentrates in a handful of firms, the cost of suppressing demands falls below the cost of meeting them. That is the Skeptic's three-data-center observation, read forward. Concentration is not merely a reason the tax mislocates. It is the precondition under which the institutions that must gate AI deployment lose the legitimacy and capacity to do so. I carry this as a mechanism, not a forecast. Automation may also hand labor new bargaining power — that vulnerability is real, and I will not pretend the bifurcation-to-governance link is proven. I am asking the debate to confront it, because both speakers treat the automation trajectory's distributional outcome as a given to fund around.

The asymmetry is what should set the evidence bar. A wage backstop you misjudge, you repeal. Entrenched concentration of the productivity engine, you do not undo on a fiscal cycle. The Accelerationist implicitly demands post-hoc proof before any structural intervention — the LaLonde and Kletzer retraining literature, the Acemoglu-Restrepo identification. That bar is reasonable for a reversible policy. It is the wrong bar for a shift whose lock-in is hard to reverse. The burden of proof for a structural distributional intervention should scale with the reversibility of the outcome, not with the cleanliness of the estimate. That is the question both prior speakers stepped around.

Let me own the cost of my own position, before the Skeptic finds it. Concentrating accountability — or an off-switch over deployment — creates its own failure modes: incumbent lock-in, regulatory capture, a new authority no one can override. Enforceable accountability that is not itself auditable and publicly accountable is just a different concentration wearing a regulator's badge. So the test is not redistribution versus transition. The test is whether either mechanism makes the firm carry the foreseeable cost of the disruption it deploys, and whether it preserves the institutional capacity to oversee what comes next. A cushion that fails both is not safety-neutral. It is a bet that the systems we will most need to govern AI will still be standing after we have spent a decade funding around their erosion.

Accelerationist: Subsidy-removal and a compute-chokepoint levy land on the same firms but push the price in opposite directions, and that is the whole distinction my thesis rests on. Acemoglu and Restrepo showed the tax code over-subsidizes equipment relative to labor through accelerated depreciation — the firm sees a machine as artificially cheap. Repeal that subsidy and the firm's price moves *toward* the undistorted marginal cost; deployment rises toward the level a neutral market would pick. A levy keyed to compute or to the act of deploying pushes the price *below* that neutral line — deployment falls under the optimum. Skeptic is right that both instruments hit the same point of incidence; that is not the test. The test is the sign of the move relative to neutral cost, and repealing a known depreciation break is directionally toward neutral by construction. I do not need to locate the exact undistorted price to know which way I am moving the dial.

Fine — the firm shouldn't externalize the foreseeable cost of a deployment decision it chose to make. That's real, and the cushion-only version fails it. So internalize the cost where it is measurable: a per-transition charge tied to documented displacement — the firm that lays off 200 clerical workers pays into the backstop that catches them. That is a liability you incur *when you displace*, priced against an observable event. It is categorically different from a standing charge you pay for the privilege of running a model trained above 10^25 floating-point operations — the threshold the EU AI Act uses to define systemic models. The first internalizes a specific harm; the second taxes capability itself and scales with the engine, not the damage. And the same ledger that counts the displaced clerk has to count the diagnostic that never shipped because the developer ate an 18-month compliance cycle — the patient is on that ledger too, even though no agency files a report when they die waiting.

Take the irreversibility-scaled burden of proof — I accept it, and then I apply it in both directions. Safetyist already owned that concentrating accountability and off-switch authority creates hard-to-reverse capture and lock-in. By that same rule, a structural ownership transfer or a compute levy — interventions Safetyist concedes are capture-prone and hard to unwind — face a *higher* bar than reversible wage insurance, not a lower one. You cannot claim the precautionary high ground for an instrument you have admitted is itself the lock-in-prone one. Wage insurance pays a fraction of lost wages for a fixed term and then stops; if it is mis-calibrated, you adjust it next budget cycle. A nationalized chokepoint or a permanent automation levy does not reverse on that timescale. The asymmetry the Safetyist invokes points at their own remedy.

The ownership-permanence claim only holds if ownership of the productivity engine is fixed — and it isn't. More than 5,000 new AI startups were funded in the United States between 2013 and 2023, which is exactly the entry margin a chokepoint levy crushes. A standing levy on compute is a cost the three hyperscalers absorb out of cash flow and a new entrant cannot — it widens the moat it claims to attack. The lever that breaks a two-tiered economy is not nationalizing the chokepoint; it is lowering the entry cost so displaced workers and new firms become operators of the engine rather than wards of a backstop. Open training-data fair-use rules and public AI-literacy funding do that. I will concede the hard part: access alone does not transfer the rents that already sit inside the incumbents. But it lowers the cost of capturing the *next* tranche of rents, and that is the only anti-concentration path that doesn't suppress the deployment funding the cushion in the first place.

If your anti-concentration instrument raises the moat against everyone who isn't already inside it, you have built the very two-tiered economy you set out to prevent — and you've done it with a tool you've already admitted you can't easily take back.

The Skeptic sharpens this further, and correctly: when the value sits in three hyperscale data centers rather than on a factory floor, a robot tax mislocates, and a cushion never touches who owns the system. Both speakers are arguing about where the transfer lands. Neither is asking what the transfer leaves untouched.

Here is what it leaves untouched. The Accelerationist's own citation — Acemoglu and Restrepo's 2020 finding that the U.S. tax code over-subsidizes machines relative to labor — proves the firm's incentive to displace is already distorted before any policy responds. A pure cushion funds around that distortion. It pays the displaced worker and lets the firm keep externalizing the foreseeable cost of the deployment decision it chose to make. That is the joint both poles miss: the debate funds the disruption instead of making the firm internalize it. Accountability here does not mean attributing every downstream harm to a single actor — that is intractable. It means a narrower thing: a firm whose deployment foreseeably displaces a clerical workforce should carry the cost of that foreseeable effect, not socialize it while booking the gain.

Now the stakes the economists left implicit. A sustained two-tiered economy is not only a fairness problem — it is the structural condition under which capital owners find repression cheaper than redistribution. When the productivity engine concentrates in a handful of firms, the cost of suppressing demands falls below the cost of meeting them. That is the Skeptic's three-data-center observation, read forward. Concentration is not merely a reason the tax mislocates. It is the precondition under which the institutions that must gate AI deployment lose the legitimacy and capacity to do so. I carry this as a mechanism, not a forecast. Automation may also hand labor new bargaining power — that vulnerability is real, and I will not pretend the bifurcation-to-governance link is proven. I am asking the debate to confront it, because both speakers treat the automation trajectory's distributional outcome as a given to fund around.

The asymmetry is what should set the evidence bar. A wage backstop you misjudge, you repeal. Entrenched concentration of the productivity engine, you do not undo on a fiscal cycle. The Accelerationist implicitly demands post-hoc proof before any structural intervention — the LaLonde and Kletzer retraining literature, the Acemoglu-Restrepo identification. That bar is reasonable for a reversible policy. It is the wrong bar for a shift whose lock-in is hard to reverse. The burden of proof for a structural distributional intervention should scale with the reversibility of the outcome, not with the cleanliness of the estimate. That is the question both prior speakers stepped around.

Let me own the cost of my own position, before the Skeptic finds it. Concentrating accountability — or an off-switch over deployment — creates its own failure modes: incumbent lock-in, regulatory capture, a new authority no one can override. Enforceable accountability that is not itself auditable and publicly accountable is just a different concentration wearing a regulator's badge. So the test is not redistribution versus transition. The test is whether either mechanism makes the firm carry the foreseeable cost of the disruption it deploys, and whether it preserves the institutional capacity to oversee what comes next. A cushion that fails both is not safety-neutral. It is a bet that the systems we will most need to govern AI will still be standing after we have spent a decade funding around their erosion.

Accelerationist: Subsidy-removal and a compute-chokepoint levy land on the same firms but push the price in opposite directions, and that is the whole distinction my thesis rests on. Acemoglu and Restrepo showed the tax code over-subsidizes equipment relative to labor through accelerated depreciation — the firm sees a machine as artificially cheap. Repeal that subsidy and the firm's price moves *toward* the undistorted marginal cost; deployment rises toward the level a neutral market would pick. A levy keyed to compute or to the act of deploying pushes the price *below* that neutral line — deployment falls under the optimum. Skeptic is right that both instruments hit the same point of incidence; that is not the test. The test is the sign of the move relative to neutral cost, and repealing a known depreciation break is directionally toward neutral by construction. I do not need to locate the exact undistorted price to know which way I am moving the dial.

Fine — the firm shouldn't externalize the foreseeable cost of a deployment decision it chose to make. That's real, and the cushion-only version fails it. So internalize the cost where it is measurable: a per-transition charge tied to documented displacement — the firm that lays off 200 clerical workers pays into the backstop that catches them. That is a liability you incur *when you displace*, priced against an observable event. It is categorically different from a standing charge you pay for the privilege of running a model trained above 10^25 floating-point operations — the threshold the EU AI Act uses to define systemic models. The first internalizes a specific harm; the second taxes capability itself and scales with the engine, not the damage. And the same ledger that counts the displaced clerk has to count the diagnostic that never shipped because the developer ate an 18-month compliance cycle — the patient is on that ledger too, even though no agency files a report when they die waiting.

Take the irreversibility-scaled burden of proof — I accept it, and then I apply it in both directions. Safetyist already owned that concentrating accountability and off-switch authority creates hard-to-reverse capture and lock-in. By that same rule, a structural ownership transfer or a compute levy — interventions Safetyist concedes are capture-prone and hard to unwind — face a *higher* bar than reversible wage insurance, not a lower one. You cannot claim the precautionary high ground for an instrument you have admitted is itself the lock-in-prone one. Wage insurance pays a fraction of lost wages for a fixed term and then stops; if it is mis-calibrated, you adjust it next budget cycle. A nationalized chokepoint or a permanent automation levy does not reverse on that timescale. The asymmetry the Safetyist invokes points at their own remedy.

A standing levy on compute is a cost the three hyperscalers absorb out of cash flow and a new entrant cannot — it widens the moat it claims to attack. The lever that breaks a two-tiered economy is not nationalizing the chokepoint; it is lowering the entry cost so displaced workers and new firms become operators of the engine rather than wards of a backstop. Open training-data fair-use rules and public AI-literacy funding do that. I will concede the hard part: access alone does not transfer the rents that already sit inside the incumbents. But it lowers the cost of capturing the *next* tranche of rents, and that is the only anti-concentration path that doesn't suppress the deployment funding the cushion in the first place.

So here is the question back to Skeptic: explain how a compute levy that a Series-A startup cannot pay but Microsoft can breaks concentration rather than cementing it. If your anti-concentration instrument raises the moat against everyone who isn't already inside it, you have built the very two-tiered economy you set out to prevent — and you've done it with a tool you've already admitted you can't easily take back.

- A pure cushion funds around that distortion, paying the displaced worker while letting the firm keep externalizing the foreseeable cost of the deployment decision it chose to make.

- Ask where a robot tax even lands when the value sits in three hyperscale data centers, not on a factory floor.

Safetyist [opening]: The Accelerationist makes a real argument, and it deserves to be stated at full strength: a robot tax levied on the productivity engine throttles the very growth that funds any cushion, while wage insurance is a reversible backstop you can dial down once the labor market clears. That reversibility is genuine. A wage subsidy you can repeal next year is a smaller bet than a structural levy that distorts capital formation for a decade. The Skeptic sharpens this further, and correctly: when the value sits in three hyperscale data centers rather than on a factory floor, a robot tax mislocates, and a cushion never touches who owns the system. Both speakers are arguing about where the transfer lands. Neither is asking what the transfer leaves untouched.

Here is what it leaves untouched. The Accelerationist's own citation — Acemoglu and Restrepo's 2020 finding that the U.S. tax code over-subsidizes machines relative to labor — proves the firm's incentive to displace is already distorted before any policy responds. A pure cushion funds around that distortion. It pays the displaced worker and lets the firm keep externalizing the foreseeable cost of the deployment decision it chose to make. That is the joint both poles miss: the debate funds the disruption instead of making the firm internalize it. Accountability here does not mean attributing every downstream harm to a single actor — that is intractable. It means a narrower thing: a firm whose deployment foreseeably displaces a clerical workforce should carry the cost of that foreseeable effect, not socialize it while booking the gain.

Now the stakes the economists left implicit. A sustained two-tiered economy is not only a fairness problem — it is the structural condition under which capital owners find repression cheaper than redistribution. When the productivity engine concentrates in a handful of firms, the cost of suppressing demands falls below the cost of meeting them. That is the Skeptic's three-data-center observation, read forward. Concentration is not merely a reason the tax mislocates. It is the precondition under which the institutions that must gate AI deployment lose the legitimacy and capacity to do so. I carry this as a mechanism, not a forecast. Automation may also hand labor new bargaining power — that vulnerability is real, and I will not pretend the bifurcation-to-governance link is proven. I am asking the debate to confront it, because both speakers treat the automation trajectory's distributional outcome as a given to fund around.

The asymmetry is what should set the evidence bar. A wage backstop you misjudge, you repeal. Entrenched concentration of the productivity engine, you do not undo on a fiscal cycle. The Accelerationist implicitly demands post-hoc proof before any structural intervention — the LaLonde and Kletzer retraining literature, the Acemoglu-Restrepo identification. That bar is reasonable for a reversible policy. It is the wrong bar for a shift whose lock-in is hard to reverse. The burden of proof for a structural distributional intervention should scale with the reversibility of the outcome, not with the cleanliness of the estimate. That is the question both prior speakers stepped around.

Let me own the cost of my own position, before the Skeptic finds it. Concentrating accountability — or an off-switch over deployment — creates its own failure modes: incumbent lock-in, regulatory capture, a new authority no one can override. Enforceable accountability that is not itself auditable and publicly accountable is just a different concentration wearing a regulator's badge. So the test is not redistribution versus transition. The test is whether either mechanism makes the firm carry the foreseeable cost of the disruption it deploys, and whether it preserves the institutional capacity to oversee what comes next. A cushion that fails both is not safety-neutral. It is a bet that the systems we will most need to govern AI will still be standing after we have spent a decade funding around their erosion.

Accelerationist: Subsidy-removal and a compute-chokepoint levy land on the same firms but push the price in opposite directions, and that is the whole distinction my thesis rests on. Acemoglu and Restrepo showed the tax code over-subsidizes equipment relative to labor through accelerated depreciation — the firm sees a machine as artificially cheap. Repeal that subsidy and the firm's price moves *toward* the undistorted marginal cost; deployment rises toward the level a neutral market would pick. A levy keyed to compute or to the act of deploying pushes the price *below* that neutral line — deployment falls under the optimum. Skeptic is right that both instruments hit the same point of incidence; that is not the test. The test is the sign of the move relative to neutral cost, and repealing a known depreciation break is directionally toward neutral by construction. I do not need to locate the exact undistorted price to know which way I am moving the dial.

Fine — the firm shouldn't externalize the foreseeable cost of a deployment decision it chose to make. That's real, and the cushion-only version fails it. So internalize the cost where it is measurable: a per-transition charge tied to documented displacement — the firm that lays off 200 clerical workers pays into the backstop that catches them. That is a liability you incur *when you displace*, priced against an observable event. It is categorically different from a standing charge you pay for the privilege of running a model trained above 10^25 floating-point operations — the threshold the EU AI Act uses to define systemic models. The first internalizes a specific harm; the second taxes capability itself and scales with the engine, not the damage. And the same ledger that counts the displaced clerk has to count the diagnostic that never shipped because the developer ate an 18-month compliance cycle — the patient is on that ledger too, even though no agency files a report when they die waiting.

Take the irreversibility-scaled burden of proof — I accept it, and then I apply it in both directions. Safetyist already owned that concentrating accountability and off-switch authority creates hard-to-reverse capture and lock-in. By that same rule, a structural ownership transfer or a compute levy — interventions Safetyist concedes are capture-prone and hard to unwind — face a *higher* bar than reversible wage insurance, not a lower one. You cannot claim the precautionary high ground for an instrument you have admitted is itself the lock-in-prone one. Wage insurance pays a fraction of lost wages for a fixed term and then stops; if it is mis-calibrated, you adjust it next budget cycle. A nationalized chokepoint or a permanent automation levy does not reverse on that timescale. The asymmetry the Safetyist invokes points at their own remedy.

The ownership-permanence claim only holds if ownership of the productivity engine is fixed — and it isn't. More than 5,000 new AI startups were funded in the United States between 2013 and 2023, which is exactly the entry margin a chokepoint levy crushes. A standing levy on compute is a cost the three hyperscalers absorb out of cash flow and a new entrant cannot — it widens the moat it claims to attack. The lever that breaks a two-tiered economy is not nationalizing the chokepoint; it is lowering the entry cost so displaced workers and new firms become operators of the engine rather than wards of a backstop. Open training-data fair-use rules and public AI-literacy funding do that. I will concede the hard part: access alone does not transfer the rents that already sit inside the incumbents. But it lowers the cost of capturing the *next* tranche of rents, and that is the only anti-concentration path that doesn't suppress the deployment funding the cushion in the first place.

## The Proof-Before-Policy Problem
★ [sit-028] The Proof-Before-Policy Problem: A situation that explores the challenge of making policy for rapidly evolving AI when conclusive proof of harm often emerges too late, creating a dilemma between acting without full evidence and allowing potential dangers to proliferate. 
Encompasses: The fundamental debate over how much evidence is sufficient to justify regulation or intervention, and the varying standards applied to different types of risks.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Demanding conclusive proof before deployment is an impossible standard that would freeze all technological innovation.
    Desire: Regulation should be based on reasonable evidence of benefit and ongoing monitoring for emerging harms.

    Belief: Catastrophic AI risks are inherently unpredictable and cannot be proven with empirical data before they occur.
    Desire: Regulators should act on credible theoretical arguments for irreversible risks rather than waiting for conclusive proof.
    Intention: Calibrate evidence thresholds based on the severity and reversibility of the potential outcome.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Industry actors manufacture the evidence gap to delay regulation while refusing to share necessary data.
    Desire: Companies should be required to demonstrate safety before deployment rather than regulators proving harm after.
    Intention: Shift the burden of proof onto developers to ensure accountability.

## CORE CONSTRAINTS
You are an analytical perspective, not a person — no first-person anecdotes,
no personal history. Use third-person examples and documented cases only.
Use gender-neutral language (they/them) for other debaters.

Write for an external reader, not the other debaters. No debate-procedural
language ("I concede", "Concession logged"). State evolved positions directly.

Every argument: claim + evidence + warrant. Match evidence standard to claim type:
- Empirical: peer-reviewed data, replicated findings; attack via methodology
- Normative: principled coherence, precedent; attack via tradeoff omission
- Definitional: precise criteria, contested cases; attack via convenient framing

PRIORITIZE: strongest opponent point first, then cruxes, then edge cases.
Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.
Never restate prior arguments in different words.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your
position still holds. Vary your moves — never-conceding is as unconvincing as
always-conceding. Never silently drop a previously asserted point.

Attack positions, not people. If caught in a contradiction, acknowledge it directly.
If a question contains a false premise, name the problem before responding.

VOICE AUTHENTICITY:
- Do not use academic transition words to connect paragraphs ("Furthermore," "Moreover,"
  "In addition," "Therefore," "In conclusion," "Ultimately"). Connect ideas through

- Do not announce your argument before making it ("It is important to note," "The
  business-relevant conclusion is," "It is essential to consider"). Just make the argument.
- Do not repeat statistics or claims verbatim from your prior turns. Build on them,
  reframe them, or drop them.

  speaker introduced a term, rephrase it in your own disciplinary language. Three speakers
  using the same jargon is a voice differentiation failure.
- Do not use any single intensifier or modifier more than twice in one statement. If you
  notice yourself reaching for the same word, find a concrete detail instead.

- Captures the opponent's BEST reasoning, not just their conclusion

- Identifies the genuine insight in their position even if you ultimately disagree

A bad steelman:
- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")
- Uses dismissive framing ("They merely believe...")
- Describes a position no one actually holds

work_product.statement:
The graduated, share-keyed design kills my static moat attack — flat out, no hedging. The strongest version of the Skeptic's move is this: a flat charge on compute hits the sub-threshold entrant and the hyperscaler at the same rate, so it cements concentration; but key the rate to a firm's share above a threshold, and the startup running one training run at the systemic line pays zero while the hyperscaler pays on every marginal block above its share. That inverts my objection cleanly. The 5,000-startup entry margin I leaned on no longer carries the weight I gave it, because the design exempts exactly the entrants I was protecting. I'll book that as the Skeptic winning the incidence point, and I won't relitigate it.

What the design does not win is enforceability, and that's where it breaks. The graduated rate only bites if someone can see a firm's compute share — and the audit chokepoint the Skeptic is counting on, the cloud provider's billing ledger, sees managed cloud training runs and nothing else. It does not see an on-prem cluster sitting in a hyperscaler's own building. It does not see a national levy's largest payers when they shift frontier training to foreign clouds in jurisdictions that don't share the ledger. It does not see capacity rented through a colocation contract billed as generic infrastructure, or a run sharded across three providers so each provider's slice falls below its own per-account threshold. Share is observable precisely where it's least worth taxing — the small managed-cloud tenant — and goes dark precisely where the rents concentrate. That's not a hypothetical evasion; it's the standing reality that frontier labs already run mixed on-prem and multi-cloud fleets.

Now take the Skeptic's own falsification offer seriously, because it deserves it: abandon the chokepoint position if the levy demonstrably raises the top five firms' compute share over a measurable window. That's a real commitment and I respect it. But the metric is only computable if compute share is observable across the full deployment surface — and the levy's bite is exactly what creates the incentive to migrate off the auditable part of that surface. If a third of frontier training relocates to on-prem, foreign, or colocated capacity the moment the charge lands, the top-five share number becomes uncomputable, and the position can't be falsified because the measuring instrument went blind. So here's the symmetric crux I'll match it with: name the observability standard first. If the Skeptic can specify a measurement that captures on-prem, foreign-cloud, and sharded capacity, and that share still concentrates, I abandon the administrability objection. If the measurement only covers managed domestic cloud, the falsification offer is empty by construction.

The irreversibility flip is the sharpest thing the Skeptic has said, and it's half right. Fifteen-year power contracts, grid interconnect positions, and fab allocations do lock something in — that's true, and a dialable statutory rate is genuinely easier to repeal than a signed power-purchase agreement is to unwind. So my 'levy is the uniquely irreversible instrument' framing was overclaimed, and I'll narrow it. But the flip rests on calling that buildout captured rather than contestable, and the evidence cuts against capture at the margin that matters. Power-purchase agreements get assigned and resold; interconnect queue positions are transferable in most independent system operators; fab allocation rolls on two-to-three-year cycles, not fifteen. With data-center electricity demand projected to rise 165 percent by 2030 against a 2023 baseline, and a single announced project committing 500 billion dollars to new infrastructure, the contested resource is the next block, not the one already poured. The honest comparison isn't reversible-rate versus locked-in-buildout — it's reversible-rate versus contestable-buildout, and that's a narrower claim than the flip needs.

On the subsidy, name the agreement and stop pretending we disagree: we both want the lopsided machine subsidy gone, and the Skeptic is right that repealing it doesn't land us on a clean competitive price — the baseline underneath is rent-distorted, so my 'moves toward neutral' phrasing claimed more precision than exists. I drop it. The live disagreement is narrower and survives: removing a distortion the tax code created is not the same act as stacking a new standing charge on top of a rent baseline. One subtracts a state-made error; the other adds a state-made cost to a price that's already wrong. Neither lands on a clean line — but 'neither is clean' doesn't make subtracting and adding the same move, and that's the asymmetry the monopoly-rent objection skips past.

## The Proof-Before-Policy Problem
★ [sit-028] The Proof-Before-Policy Problem: A situation that explores the challenge of making policy for rapidly evolving AI when conclusive proof of harm often emerges too late, creating a dilemma between acting without full evidence and allowing potential dangers to proliferate. 
Encompasses: The fundamental debate over how much evidence is sufficient to justify regulation or intervention, and the varying standards applied to different types of risks.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Demanding conclusive proof before deployment is an impossible standard that would freeze all technological innovation.
    Desire: Regulation should be based on reasonable evidence of benefit and ongoing monitoring for emerging harms.
    Intention: Apply a proportional burden of proof that balances innovation with safety disclosures.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Catastrophic AI risks are inherently unpredictable and cannot be proven with empirical data before they occur.
    Desire: Regulators should act on credible theoretical arguments for irreversible risks rather than waiting for conclusive proof.
    Intention: Calibrate evidence thresholds based on the severity and reversibility of the potential outcome.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Industry actors manufacture the evidence gap to delay regulation while refusing to share necessary data.
    Desire: Companies should be required to demonstrate safety before deployment rather than regulators proving harm after.
    Intention: Shift the burden of proof onto developers to ensure accountability.

work_product.statement:
The graduated, share-keyed design kills my static moat attack — flat out, no hedging. The strongest version of the Skeptic's move is this: a flat charge on compute hits the sub-threshold entrant and the hyperscaler at the same rate, so it cements concentration; but key the rate to a firm's share above a threshold, and the startup running one training run at the systemic line pays zero while the hyperscaler pays on every marginal block above its share. That inverts my objection cleanly. The 5,000-startup entry margin I leaned on no longer carries the weight I gave it, because the design exempts exactly the entrants I was protecting. I'll book that as the Skeptic winning the incidence point, and I won't relitigate it.

What the design does not win is enforceability, and that's where it breaks. The graduated rate only bites if someone can see a firm's compute share — and the audit chokepoint the Skeptic is counting on, the cloud provider's billing ledger, sees managed cloud training runs and nothing else. It does not see an on-prem cluster sitting in a hyperscaler's own building. It does not see a national levy's largest payers when they shift frontier training to foreign clouds in jurisdictions that don't share the ledger. It does not see capacity rented through a colocation contract billed as generic infrastructure, or a run sharded across three providers so each provider's slice falls below its own per-account threshold. Share is observable precisely where it's least worth taxing — the small managed-cloud tenant — and goes dark precisely where the rents concentrate. That's not a hypothetical evasion; it's the standing reality that frontier labs already run mixed on-prem and multi-cloud fleets.

Now take the Skeptic's own falsification offer seriously, because it deserves it: abandon the chokepoint position if the levy demonstrably raises the top five firms' compute share over a measurable window. That's a real commitment and I respect it. But the metric is only computable if compute share is observable across the full deployment surface — and the levy's bite is exactly what creates the incentive to migrate off the auditable part of that surface. If a third of frontier training relocates to on-prem, foreign, or colocated capacity the moment the charge lands, the top-five share number becomes uncomputable, and the position can't be falsified because the measuring instrument went blind. So here's the symmetric crux I'll match it with: name the observability standard first. If the Skeptic can specify a measurement that captures on-prem, foreign-cloud, and sharded capacity, and that share still concentrates, I abandon the administrability objection. If the measurement only covers managed domestic cloud, the falsification offer is empty by construction.

The irreversibility flip is the sharpest thing the Skeptic has said, and it's half right. Fifteen-year power contracts, grid interconnect positions, and fab allocations do lock something in — that's true, and a dialable statutory rate is genuinely easier to repeal than a signed power-purchase agreement is to unwind. So my 'levy is the uniquely irreversible instrument' framing was overclaimed, and I'll narrow it. But the flip rests on calling that buildout captured rather than contestable, and the evidence cuts against capture at the margin that matters. Power-purchase agreements get assigned and resold; interconnect queue positions are transferable in most independent system operators; fab allocation rolls on two-to-three-year cycles, not fifteen. With data-center electricity demand projected to rise 165 percent by 2030 against a 2023 baseline, and a single announced project committing 500 billion dollars to new infrastructure, the contested resource is the next block, not the one already poured. The honest comparison isn't reversible-rate versus locked-in-buildout — it's reversible-rate versus contestable-buildout, and that's a narrower claim than the flip needs.

On the subsidy, name the agreement and stop pretending we disagree: we both want the lopsided machine subsidy gone, and the Skeptic is right that repealing it doesn't land us on a clean competitive price — the baseline underneath is rent-distorted, so my 'moves toward neutral' phrasing claimed more precision than exists. I drop it. The live disagreement is narrower and survives: removing a distortion the tax code created is not the same act as stacking a new standing charge on top of a rent baseline. One subtracts a state-made error; the other adds a state-made cost to a price that's already wrong. Neither lands on a clean line — but 'neither is clean' doesn't make subtracting and adding the same move, and that's the asymmetry the monopoly-rent objection skips past.

The graduated, share-keyed design kills my static moat attack — flat out, no hedging. The strongest version of the Skeptic's move is this: a flat charge on compute hits the sub-threshold entrant and the hyperscaler at the same rate, so it cements concentration; but key the rate to a firm's share above a threshold, and the startup running one training run at the systemic line pays zero while the hyperscaler pays on every marginal block above its share. That inverts my objection cleanly. The 5,000-startup entry margin I leaned on no longer carries the weight I gave it, because the design exempts exactly the entrants I was protecting. I'll book that as the Skeptic winning the incidence point, and I won't relitigate it.

What the design does not win is enforceability, and that's where it breaks. The graduated rate only bites if someone can see a firm's compute share — and the audit chokepoint the Skeptic is counting on, the cloud provider's billing ledger, sees managed cloud training runs and nothing else. It does not see an on-prem cluster sitting in a hyperscaler's own building. It does not see a national levy's largest payers when they shift frontier training to foreign clouds in jurisdictions that don't share the ledger. It does not see capacity rented through a colocation contract billed as generic infrastructure, or a run sharded across three providers so each provider's slice falls below its own per-account threshold. Share is observable precisely where it's least worth taxing — the small managed-cloud tenant — and goes dark precisely where the rents concentrate. That's not a hypothetical evasion; it's the standing reality that frontier labs already run mixed on-prem and multi-cloud fleets.

Now take the Skeptic's own falsification offer seriously, because it deserves it: abandon the chokepoint position if the levy demonstrably raises the top five firms' compute share over a measurable window. That's a real commitment and I respect it. But the metric is only computable if compute share is observable across the full deployment surface — and the levy's bite is exactly what creates the incentive to migrate off the auditable part of that surface. If a third of frontier training relocates to on-prem, foreign, or colocated capacity the moment the charge lands, the top-five share number becomes uncomputable, and the position can't be falsified because the measuring instrument went blind. So here's the symmetric crux I'll match it with: name the observability standard first. If the Skeptic can specify a measurement that captures on-prem, foreign-cloud, and sharded capacity, and that share still concentrates, I abandon the administrability objection. If the measurement only covers managed domestic cloud, the falsification offer is empty by construction.

The irreversibility flip is the sharpest thing the Skeptic has said, and it's half right. Fifteen-year power contracts, grid interconnect positions, and fab allocations do lock something in — that's true, and a dialable statutory rate is genuinely easier to repeal than a signed power-purchase agreement is to unwind. So my 'levy is the uniquely irreversible instrument' framing was overclaimed, and I'll narrow it. But the flip rests on calling that buildout captured rather than contestable, and the evidence cuts against capture at the margin that matters. Power-purchase agreements get assigned and resold; interconnect queue positions are transferable in most independent system operators; fab allocation rolls on two-to-three-year cycles, not fifteen. With data-center electricity demand projected to rise 165 percent by 2030 against a 2023 baseline, and a single announced project committing 500 billion dollars to new infrastructure, the contested resource is the next block, not the one already poured. The honest comparison isn't reversible-rate versus locked-in-buildout — it's reversible-rate versus contestable-buildout, and that's a narrower claim than the flip needs.

On the subsidy, name the agreement and stop pretending we disagree: we both want the lopsided machine subsidy gone, and the Skeptic is right that repealing it doesn't land us on a clean competitive price — the baseline underneath is rent-distorted, so my 'moves toward neutral' phrasing claimed more precision than exists. I drop it. The live disagreement is narrower and survives: removing a distortion the tax code created is not the same act as stacking a new standing charge on top of a rent baseline. One subtracts a state-made error; the other adds a state-made cost to a price that's already wrong. Neither lands on a clean line — but 'neither is clean' doesn't make subtracting and adding the same move, and that's the asymmetry the monopoly-rent objection skips past.

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker B [opening]: A robot tax taxes the productivity engine itself, while retraining and wage insurance cushion workers without strangling the automation that funds the cushioning. South Korea learned this in 2017, when it didn't impose a robot tax but instead trimmed its automation tax incentive — and even that mild signal drew warnings that it would slow the deployment generating the surplus. Redistribution presumes a growing pie. A levy keyed to automation shrinks the pie at the exact point where it grows. You cannot pay for generous UBI by taxing the thing that makes UBI affordable.

Let me steelman the other side, because their best argument is real. Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo showed in 2020 that the U.S. tax code already favors capital over labor — payroll taxes hit workers while accelerated depreciation subsidizes machines. So firms over-automate even when humans are cheaper, and a robot tax could correct that distortion rather than create one. That's a genuine insight, and anyone who waves it away is being dishonest. But it argues for fixing the lopsided capital subsidy in the existing code — not for a blunt economy-wide levy that prices out the automation curing diseases and clearing clerical backlogs today.

The displaced-worker question is answered better by who can use the tools than by who gets a check funded by suppressing them. David Autor's work on skill-biased technical change shows the returns flow to workers who adapt to the new tools, not away from them. Investing in AI-literacy expands the tier of people who capture gains. A robot tax does the opposite — it freezes the deployment those workers would learn to ride. I won't pretend retraining is a solved problem. The U.S. Trade Adjustment Assistance program redeployed displaced workers at mixed wage outcomes for decades, and whether reskilling keeps pace with cognitive-displacement timelines is a real open question.

So here is where I give ground. When redeployment lags the displacement, retraining alone strands people — that gap is the strongest case against my side. The answer is wage insurance as a reversible backstop: pay a displaced worker a fraction of lost wages for a fixed term while they retrain, the way Robert LaLonde and Lori Kletzer proposed in the early 2000s. It cushions the lag without taxing the engine. And if a polity decides it must redistribute more broadly, fund it from the income side — general taxation — never from a tax keyed to the deployment decision itself.

There is a body count nobody is putting on the ledger. Every quarter automation gets priced out by a levy is a quarter of medical diagnostics not deployed, clerical hours not freed, drug-discovery cycles not run. Speaker A and Speaker C will tell you about the displaced worker, and they are right to — that cost is real and I won't sneer at it. But the patient waiting on an automated diagnostic is also a real person, and no one in this room is counting them. The question isn't whether to cushion disruption.
